To intimidate someone means to make them feel afraid, nervous, or powerless — often on purpose — so that they lose their confidence, feel controlled, or end up doing what you want (or stop doing what they were going to do).

The heart of the word is this: the intimidated person feels smaller and weaker than the intimidator, and that feeling controls their behavior.

1. Deliberate intimidation — using fear as a tool

This is the most common and serious use of the word. Here, someone intentionally tries to frighten another person to get a specific result. The intimidator wants the other person to back down, stay quiet, give up, or obey.

"The gang tried to intimidate the witness into staying silent." "The corrupt official intimidated journalists so they wouldn't publish the story."

Notice the pattern: fear is being used as a weapon. The goal isn't just to scare — it's to control.

2. Unintentional intimidation — feeling overwhelmed or small

Sometimes, a person (or even a situation) can intimidate you without trying to at all. This happens when someone's talent, authority, reputation, or presence makes you feel nervous or inadequate — even though they are not threatening you in any way.

"The professor's vast knowledge intimidated the new student, who was too nervous to ask questions." "She felt intimidated by the long list of job requirements." "The sheer size of the mountain intimidated the beginner hiker."

In these cases, nobody is trying to frighten anyone. The student isn't being threatened. But the feeling is the same — a loss of confidence, a sense of being overpowered. This is why the word fits both situations.

Whether the intimidation is intentional or not, the experience of the person being intimidated is always the same: they feel a rise of fear or nervousness and a loss of freedom to act normally. They might feel too small to speak up, too pressured to push back, or too overwhelmed to move forward. That inner shrinking — that's the signature of being intimidated.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Frighten / Scare — These simply cause sudden fear, often by accident (a loud noise frightens you). Intimidation is different because it makes someone feel overpowered or controlled, not just startled. Intimidation lingers and shapes behavior; fright is often just a moment.

Threaten — To threaten someone is to make an explicit warning of harm: "Do this or else." Intimidation is broader and subtler — you can intimidate someone through your tone, your size, your reputation, or your authority, without ever making a direct threat.

Bully — Bullying is a repeated pattern of intimidation and harm, typically aimed at someone weaker. Intimidation can be a single act. Every bully intimidates, but not every act of intimidation is bullying.

Pressure — Pressuring someone means pushing them to do something, but it doesn't always involve fear. Intimidation always involves a fear or powerlessness element.

Learning how a word behaves in a sentence is as important as knowing its meaning.

Intimidate + someone — "His presence intimidated everyone in the room." (He made them all feel nervous.)

Intimidate + someone + into + [doing something] — "They intimidated her into signing the contract." (They used fear to force her to sign.)

Feel/be intimidated + by — "I felt intimidated by her confidence." (Her confidence made me feel small and nervous.)

Intimidating (adjective) — describes something or someone that causes nervousness or fear. "The interview panel was intimidating."

Intimidated (adjective) — describes the person who feels afraid or overwhelmed as a result. "He walked in feeling intimidated."

Intimidation (noun) — the act itself. "The court condemned the use of intimidation against witnesses."

Intimidator (noun, less common) — a person who intimidates others. "He was a natural intimidator on the sports field."

Intimidation does not require physical danger. You can be intimidated by someone's intelligence, wealth, beauty, social status, or calm authority — none of which are physically threatening. What matters is the imbalance of power, real or imagined, that makes you feel smaller and less free. A nervous student in front of a brilliant teacher, a new employee walking into a boardroom full of executives, a beginner standing at the base of a vast mountain — all of these are genuine examples of intimidation, even without a single threat being made.

That is the full picture of this word: to intimidate is to make someone feel too small to act freely, whether through deliberate fear or simply through overwhelming presence.
